title: How to calculate the R&D tax credit for 2024
description: Calculate the 2024 R&D tax credit from qualified research expenses under IRC Section 41 using the 20% Regular or 14% Alternative Simplified Credit.
summary: Calculating the R&D tax credit for 2024 requires U.S. businesses to identify qualified research expenses under IRC Section 41, confirm activities pass the Four-Part Test, and compute the credit using either the 20% Regular Research Credit or the 14% Alternative Simplified Credit, while coordinating Section 174/174A deductions and Section 280C(c) elections on Form 6765.

body.text: Calculating the R&D tax credit for 2024 requires U.S. businesses to identify qualified research expenses under IRC Section 41, confirm activities pass the Four-Part Test, and compute the credit using either the 20% Regular Research Credit or the 14% Alternative Simplified Credit, while coordinating Section 174/174A deductions and Section 280C(c) elections on Form 6765.
1. Introduction: Calculating the U.S. R&D Tax Credit for 2024 in an Evolving Legislative and Regulatory Landscape

Calculating the United States Research and Development (R&D) tax credit for the 2024 tax year—and evaluating its ongoing interaction with 2025 and 2026 compliance transitions—requires strict adherence to Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Codified to incentivize domestic technological innovation by offsetting a portion of qualified research spending, the Section 41 credit sits at the intersection of technical scientific substantiation and multi-year financial computation. Two major legislative and administrative developments govern how taxpayers approach 2024 R&D credit calculations and subsequent amended or transitional filings:

items: Retroactive and Transitional Deductibility Relief under the OBBBA: On July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72, commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). While the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 originally forced taxpayers in the 2022 through 2024 tax years to capitalize and amortize domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures over five years under IRC Section 174, Section 70302 of the OBBBA enacted IRC Section 174A, restoring immediate deductibility for domestic R&E for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, and granting eligible small businesses a retroactive election under IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 to apply Section 174A back to the 2022–2024 tax years.

Heightened IRS Substantiation on Form 6765: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) overhauled Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, introducing Section G (Business Component Information). Under the finalized Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, released February 2026), Section G is optional for all filers for the 2024 and 2025 tax years (all tax years beginning before 2026) and becomes mandatory for most taxpayers starting in the 2026 tax year.

body.text: Analysis: Because 2024 R&D credit calculations remain open to IRS examination and retroactive Section 174A small-business amendments under Rev. Proc. 2025-28, accurate computation requires mastering four pillars: (1) underlying Section 174/174A expense eligibility and Section 280C(c) coordination; (2) activity qualification under the Section 41(d) Four-Part Test; (3) aggregation of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs); and (4) mathematical modeling between the Regular Research Credit (RRC) and the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC).
2. Underlying Expense Treatment for 2024 R&D Credit Calculations: Section 174, Section 174A, and Section 280C(c)

To include an expenditure in the calculation of the IRC Section 41 research credit for 2024, the cost must first qualify as a research or experimental (R&E) expenditure under IRC Section 174 (or, where retroactively elected for 2024 or applied post-2024, IRC Section 174A).
2.1 TCJA Capitalization Rules for 2022–2024 and the OBBBA Reversal

Prior to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, taxpayers could immediately deduct R&E expenditures in the year paid or incurred under IRC Section 174. Under the TCJA (Pub. L. 115-97), for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021—which originally governed the 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax years—specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures, explicitly including software development costs, could no longer be deducted immediately. Instead:

items: Domestic R&E expenditures had to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 5-year period (starting with the midpoint of the taxable year in which paid or incurred).
Foreign R&E expenditures had to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year period.

body.text: The enactment of the OBBBA (Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302) on July 4, 2025, added IRC Section 174A for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, as confirmed by IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 and Grant Thornton's analysis of OBBBA. Under Section 174A(a), taxpayers may once again immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures (including software development under Section 174A(d)(3)) in the taxable year paid or incurred, or alternatively elect under Section 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize them over a period of not less than 60 months (or over 10 years under IRC Section 59(e)).
2.2 Impact on 2024 Calculations: Retroactive Small Business Elections and Transition Recovery

For taxpayers calculating or amending their 2024 R&D tax credit and associated R&E deductions, the OBBBA and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (issued August 28, 2025) establish three distinct transition pathways for domestic R&E costs incurred in 2022 through 2024, while maintaining strict capitalization for foreign R&E:

items: Retroactive 2022–2024 Election for Eligible Small Businesses: Under OBBBA § 70302(f) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28, eligible small businesses meeting the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts test (average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 2025 threshold, or as applicable under § 448(c)) may elect to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021—including the 2024 tax year—by filing amended returns or administrative adjustment requests (AARs) to deduct 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs immediately instead of amortizing them.

Accelerated Recovery of Unamortized 2022–2024 Domestic R&E Costs in 2025 or 2025–2026: Taxpayers that do not make (or are ineligible for) the retroactive 2022–2024 election may elect to deduct their remaining unamortized domestic R&E basis from the 2022–2024 tax years either (a) in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (the 2025 tax year), or (b) ratably over the two-year period spanning 2025 and 2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-28; Surgent CPE OBBBA Analysis).

Continued 15-Year Amortization for Foreign R&E: Foreign R&E expenditures remain governed by IRC Section 174 and must continue to be capitalized and amortized over 15 years (and cannot be included in Section 41 QREs, which are restricted to domestic research under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F)). Furthermore, for property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, modified Section 174(d) prohibits immediate recovery of unamortized foreign R&E basis upon disposition, retirement, or abandonment (Grant Thornton; Surgent CPE).

body.text: 2.3 Coordination Between the R&D Credit and R&E Deductions under IRC Section 280C(c)

Calculating the net benefit of the R&D tax credit for 2024 requires applying the coordination rules of IRC Section 280C(c), which prevent a taxpayer from claiming both a full deduction and a full tax credit on the same dollar of research expenditure.

items: Clarification of Statutory Citation: While pre-TCJA law codified the reduced credit election in Section 280C(c)(3), the TCJA redesignated the reduced credit election as IRC Section 280C(c)(2) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 (including 2024), and the OBBBA (Pub. L. 119-21) retained the reduced credit election under IRC Section 280C(c)(2) while restoring the general deduction-reduction rule under Section 280C(c)(1) (Surgent CPE; Instructions for Form 6765).

Pathway 1 — Full Section 41 Credit with Reduced Deduction/Capitalized Amount: Under the restored Section 280C(c)(1) rule (applicable to 2024 returns where retroactive Section 174A is elected, and to all post-2024 returns), if a taxpayer claims the full gross Section 41 credit, the taxpayer must reduce its otherwise allowable domestic R&E deduction (or capitalized amount) by the full dollar amount of the research credit claimed. (For 2024 returns that remain under the TCJA capitalization regime without a retroactive OBBBA election, TCJA's version of Section 280C(c)(1) required reducing the capitalized Section 174 amount only to the extent the Section 41 credit exceeded the allowable current-year amortization deduction.)

Pathway 2 — Reduced Section 41 Credit Election under Section 280C(c)(2): Alternatively, on an original timely filed return (including extensions), a taxpayer may make an irrevocable election on Form 6765 (Item A) under IRC Section 280C(c)(2) to claim a reduced research credit. Under this election, the gross credit is reduced by the product of the gross credit multiplied by the maximum corporate tax rate (currently 21% under IRC Section 11(b), yielding a net credit equal to 79% of the gross credit). Making this election preserves 100% of the taxpayer's allowable R&E deduction without reduction (Instructions for Form 6765).

body.text: Analysis: Whether a taxpayer calculating its 2024 R&D credit should elect the reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) depends on its marginal federal and state tax rates, its Net Operating Loss (NOL) carryforward position, and whether it is a small business retroactively electing immediate 2024 expensing under Rev. Proc. 2025-28.
3. Qualifying Activities for the 2024 Calculation: The Section 41(d) Four-Part Test and Exclusions

Before any dollar of expense can enter the 2024 R&D tax credit calculation, the underlying research activity must satisfy the statutory definition of "qualified research" in IRC Section 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a).
3.1 The Statutory Four-Part Test

Every business component must independently satisfy all four criteria of the Four-Part Test. Failure to substantiate any single element disqualifies all expenses associated with that business component (IRS Aerospace Research Credit Audit Technique Guide):

items: Permitted Purpose (Section 174 / 174A & Business Component Test — IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), § 41(d)(2)(B), § 41(d)(3)): The expenditures must qualify as R&E costs under Section 174 (or Section 174A) incurred in the taxpayer's trade or business and must be undertaken to develop a new or improved business component—defined strictly as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. The activity's purpose must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(A)). Activities relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors are statutorily ineligible (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B)).

Elimination of Technical Uncertainty (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)): At the outset of the activity, the information available to the taxpayer must not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)). Routine engineering where the optimal design is already known at the outset fails this requirement.

Process of Experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all—defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities for a business component measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. A process of experimentation requires identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and conducting a systematic evaluative process (such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error) to test and analyze those alternatives.

Technological in Nature (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)): The process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Research in the social sciences, arts, humanities, economics, or market research is excluded (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(G); Instructions for Form 6765).

body.text: 3.2 Statutory Exclusions, Reverse Engineering, and the Shrink-Back Rule

Even if an activity involves technical personnel, IRC Section 41(d)(4) excludes eight categories of activities from the credit calculation, including research conducted after commercial production begins, adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement, foreign research, funded research, and the duplication of an existing business component (reverse engineering) under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)).

items: Reverse Engineering Exclusion: Reproducing an existing business component in whole or in part from a physical examination of the component itself, or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information, does not constitute qualified research because it duplicates existing knowledge rather than resolving technological uncertainty.

Application of the Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)): When an overall product or project fails the Four-Part Test (for instance, because less than 80% of the total project activities constitute experimentation, or because initial work involved excluded reverse engineering or routine adaptation), the taxpayer cannot claim the whole project. Instead, under the shrink-back rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), the Four-Part Test is reapplied to the most significant subset of elements (subcomponents) of the business component until either a subcomponent satisfies all four requirements (and its specific costs are isolated and documented) or the most basic element of the component fails to qualify.

Judicial Precedents on Component-Level Substantiation and Shrink-Back: In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (decided December 23, 2024, Docket No. 4759-22), the U.S. Tax Court disallowed Section 41 credits claimed by a mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering firm across three sampled trial projects and sustained 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 (Cherry Bekaert Analysis; Strike Tax Analysis). The Tax Court held that performing standard engineering calculations using available historical data and following a linear design process did not establish objective technical uncertainty or an iterative process of experimentation. Crucially, the court noted that while a failed overall building design could theoretically shrink back under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to a specific discipline or subcomponent, the taxpayer lacked granular, activity-level time records to segregate qualifying subcomponent experimentation from non-qualifying routine work. This aligns with Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, where the Seventh Circuit held that claiming an entire vessel under an "all or nothing" strategy without subcomponent-level documentation of the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold foreclosed applying the shrink-back rule, and contrasts with Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, where detailed project-by-project documentation substantiated 11 of 12 sampled hardware and software projects while properly excluding one project limited to routine post-commercial bug fixing and cosmetic look-and-feel modifications.

body.text: 4. Identifying and Quantifying Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) for 2024

Once qualifying business components (or shrink-back subcomponents) are verified under Section 41(d), calculating the 2024 R&D credit requires aggregating Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC Section 41(b) (comprising in-house research expenses and contract research expenses). Only amounts falling into three statutory categories (plus basic research payments to qualified organizations under Section 41(e), where applicable) may be included on Form 6765, Section F:

items: In-House Wage Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), § 41(b)(2)(B)): Taxable wages (as defined in IRC § 3401(a), i.e., Form W-2 Box 1 taxable wages, or self-employment earned income under § 401(c)(1)) paid or incurred for an employee's qualified services, which consist of:
Engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research;
Directly supervising qualified research (first-line technical management); or
Directly supporting qualified research (such as a machinist fabricating an experimental prototype part or a technician running test trials, as noted in JLK Rosenberger's Form 6765 Guidance).

The 80% "Substantially All" Wage Rule (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)): If "substantially all" (80% or more) of the services performed by an individual for the taxpayer during the 2024 taxable year consist of qualified services, then 100% of that employee's taxable wages for the taxable year qualify as QREs (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)). If an employee spends less than 80% of their time on qualified services, only the exact prorated fraction of their taxable wages attributable to qualified services may be included. Non-taxable fringe benefits (such as nontaxable health insurance premiums or employer 401(k) matching contributions) do not constitute § 3401(a) wages and must be excluded from the wage QRE calculation.

Supply Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), § 41(b)(2)(C)): Amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. "Supplies" means any tangible property other than (a) land or improvements to land, and (b) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)). Additionally, under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and the Instructions for Form 6765, amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers (such as leased cloud computing development/testing environments) directly in the conduct of qualified research are reported separately on Form 6765 as in-house research expenses. Capitalized, depreciable equipment is strictly excluded.

Contract Research Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)): In general, 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf within the United States (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A)). (Higher statutory rates of 75% apply to amounts paid to qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C), and 100% applies to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories for qualified energy research under § 41(b)(3)(D), as confirmed in the Instructions for Form 6765 and EisnerAmper.) Per Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), contract research qualifies only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, requires the research to be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and requires the taxpayer to bear the economic risk of expense even if the research is not successful.

body.text: 5. Step-by-Step Computational Mechanics for the 2024 R&D Tax Credit: RRC vs. ASC
Once a taxpayer has calculated its total 2024 QREs (reported on Form 6765, Section F, Line 48), the taxpayer must compute the credit using one of two statutory calculation methods on Form 6765:

items: Method 1: The Regular Research Credit (RRC) under IRC Section 41(a)(1) (Form 6765, Section A), or
Method 2: The Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC Section 41(c)(5) (Form 6765, Section B).

body.text: As the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) note, taxpayers eligible for both methods may compute their credit under both formulas during return preparation to determine which yields the greater tax benefit before making their filing election.
5.1 Method 1: Calculating the Regular Research Credit (RRC)

Under IRC Section 41(a)(1), the Regular Research Credit equals 20% of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year (e.g., 2024) over the base amount (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)). Calculating the RRC for 2024 requires six sequential steps:

items: Step 1 — Determine the Fixed-Base Percentage (IRC § 41(c)(3)):

Established Firms: For taxpayers that had both gross receipts and QREs during at least three taxable years in the 1984–1988 base period, the fixed-base percentage is the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989.

Start-Up Companies (IRC § 41(c)(3)(B)): If the first taxable year in which a taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs began after December 31, 1983, or if the taxpayer had fewer than three taxable years with both gross receipts and QREs during 1984–1988, the start-up rules assign a fixed-base percentage of 3% for each of the taxpayer's first 5 taxable years beginning after 1993 for which the taxpayer has QREs. Starting in the 6th through 10th such years, the percentage phases in incrementally toward the taxpayer's actual historical QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio, and from the 11th year onward, is based on actual QRE-to-gross-receipts ratios from designated five-year lookback windows.

Statutory Cap and Rounding (IRC § 41(c)(3)(C)–(D)): In no event may the fixed-base percentage exceed 16.00% (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)), and the percentage is rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1% (two decimal places).

Step 2 — Calculate Average Annual Gross Receipts for the Prior 4 Tax Years (IRC § 41(c)(1)(B)): Sum the taxpayer's gross receipts (reduced by returns and allowances under § 41(c)(7)) for the 4 taxable years immediately preceding the credit year (for a 2024 calculation, tax years 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023) and divide by 4.
Step 3 — Compute the Preliminary Base Amount (IRC § 41(c)(1)): Multiply the Fixed-Base Percentage (Step 1) by the Average Annual Gross Receipts for the prior 4 years (Step 2).

Step 4 — Apply the 50% Minimum Base Amount Floor (IRC § 41(c)(2)): Under IRC § 41(c)(2), in no event shall the base amount be less than 50% of the current credit year's QREs. Thus, the Final Base Amount is the greater of the Preliminary Base Amount (Step 3) or 50% of 2024 QREs.
Step 5 — Calculate the Creditable Excess QREs: Subtract the Final Base Amount (Step 4) from the current year's (2024) total QREs.

Step 6 — Compute the Gross Regular Research Credit (IRC § 41(a)(1)): Multiply the Creditable Excess QREs (Step 5) by 20%. (If the taxpayer elects the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2), multiply the gross credit by 79%—i.e., reduce it by 21%—to obtain the net credit.)

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: 2024 Regular Research Credit (RRC) Startup Calculation
The following hypothetical example illustrates how a startup company in its third year of having QREs calculates its 2024 RRC:

items: Hypothetical Inputs for Tax Year 2024:
2024 Total QREs = $125,000
Startup Fixed-Base Percentage (Year 3 of QREs under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(I)) = 3.00%
Step-by-Step Arithmetic Verification:
Preliminary Base Amount = 3.00% × $600,000 = $18,000
Minimum Base Amount Floor = 50% × $125,000 = $62,500
Final Base Amount = Greater of $18,000 or $62,500 = $62,500
Creditable Excess QREs = $125,000 − $62,500 = $62,500
Gross 2024 RRC = 20% × $62,500 = $12,500
Net 2024 RRC (if IRC § 280C(c)(2) reduced credit is elected at the 21% maximum corporate rate) = $12,500 − ($12,500 × 21%) = $12,500 − $2,625 = $9,875

cells: IRC § 41(c)(3)(B) startup rate (capped at 16% max under § 41(c)(3)(C))
IRC § 41(c)(1)(B): Sum of prior 4 years' gross receipts divided by 4
Fixed-Base Percentage × Average Annual Gross Receipts (3.00% × $600,000)
Greater of Preliminary Base Amount ($18,000) or Minimum Floor ($62,500)
Current-Year QREs minus Final Base Amount ($125,000 − $62,500)

body.text: 5.2 Method 2: Calculating the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC)

To eliminate the administrative burden of substantiating gross receipts and QREs from the 1984–1988 base period or tracking multi-year gross receipt growth, Congress enacted the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC Section 41(c)(5) (and regulated under 26 CFR § 1.41-9). Under the ASC, gross receipts are excluded from the formula entirely.
Election and Amended Return Rules (26 CFR § 1.41-9 and TD 9666)

items: Binding Election: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(1) and the Instructions for Form 6765, once a taxpayer elects the ASC on Form 6765 (Section B), the election applies to that taxable year and all subsequent taxable years unless revoked with the consent of the Commissioner. (A taxpayer is deemed to have requested and been granted consent to revoke an ASC election on an original timely filed return for a subsequent year simply by completing Section A for the Regular Credit on that year's Form 6765, per 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(3), though an ASC election may not be revoked on an amended return.)

Claiming the ASC on a 2024 Amended Return: Pursuant to Treasury Decision 9666 (TD 9666, 2014-26 I.R.B.) and finalized 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(2), a taxpayer may make an ASC election for a tax year (such as 2024) on an amended return, provided that the taxpayer (and no member of its controlled group) did not previously claim a Section 41 credit on an original or amended return for that tax year.

body.text: Step-by-Step ASC Formula for 2024

items: Step 1 — Determine QREs for the 3 Preceding Taxable Years (IRC § 41(c)(5)(A)): Identify total QREs for the 3 taxable years immediately preceding the credit year (for a 2024 calculation, tax years 2021, 2022, and 2023). Per 26 CFR § 1.41-9(c)(2), QREs for the prior three years must be determined on a basis consistent with the definition of QREs for the credit year.
Step 2 — Check Whether QREs Existed in All 3 Prior Years:
Standard 14% ASC Tier (IRC § 41(c)(5)(A)): If the taxpayer had positive QREs in each of the three preceding tax years (2021, 2022, and 2023):
Compute the 3-Year Average Historical QREs by summing QREs for 2021, 2022, and 2023 and dividing by 3.
Compute the ASC Base Amount by multiplying the 3-Year Average Historical QREs by 50%.
Compute the Creditable Excess QREs by subtracting the ASC Base Amount from the current year's (2024) QREs.
Multiply the Creditable Excess QREs by 14% to determine the Gross ASC.

Special 6% ASC Tier When Any Prior Year Has Zero QREs (IRC § 41(c)(5)(B); 26 CFR § 1.41-9(c)(1)): If the taxpayer had zero QREs in any one (or more) of the three preceding taxable years (2021, 2022, or 2023), the base amount calculation is bypassed entirely and the Gross ASC equals 6% of the current year's (2024) QREs.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: 2024 Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Calculation
The following hypothetical example demonstrates both tiers of the 2024 ASC calculation:

items: Scenario A (QREs in All 3 Prior Years — 14% Rate):
2024 Total QREs = $125,000
3-Year Average Historical QREs = $300,000 / 3 = $100,000
Creditable Excess QREs = $125,000 − $50,000 = $75,000
Gross 2024 ASC = 14% × $75,000 = $10,500
Net 2024 ASC (with IRC § 280C(c)(2) election at 21% corporate rate) = $10,500 × 79% = $8,295
Scenario B (Zero QREs in at Least One of 2021–2023 — 6% Rate):
Gross 2024 ASC = 6% × $125,000 = $7,500
Net 2024 ASC (with IRC § 280C(c)(2) election at 21% corporate rate) = $7,500 × 79% = $5,925

cells: IRC § 41(c)(5)(A): Sum of 2021–2023 QREs divided by 3
N/A (At least one prior year had $0 QREs)
Current-Year QREs minus ASC Base Amount ($125,000 − $50,000)
Creditable Excess QREs × Applicable Statutory Rate

body.text: Analysis — Choosing Between the RRC and the ASC for 2024: As illustrated in the tables above, when a startup or low-base-percentage company has a Preliminary Base Amount below 50% of current-year QREs, the RRC yields an effective gross credit of 10.0% of total QREs (20% × 50% = $12,500 on $125,000 of QREs), outperforming the ASC ($10,500). Conversely, for rapidly growing companies whose prior-four-year average gross receipts have expanded faster than their R&D spending—or established enterprises lacking verifiable 1984–1988 records—the RRC Preliminary Base Amount often rises sharply, making the ASC's gross-receipts-independent formula significantly more advantageous and defensible (KBKG Comparison).
6. Reporting the Calculation on IRS Form 6765: 2024–2025 Optionality vs. 2026 Mandatory Section G Disclosures

Historically, filing Form 6765 required reporting only company-wide summary totals of wages, supplies, and contract research expenses, giving the IRS no visibility into individual R&D projects unless the return was selected for audit.

Following extensive public feedback, the IRS released revised Form 6765 and finalized Instructions (Rev. December 2025, published February 2026), introducing Section G (Business Component Information) alongside revamped Sections E and F (PwC Tax Insight; EisnerAmper).
6.1 Effective Dates: Optional for 2024 and 2025, Mandatory for 2026

items: 2024 and 2025 Tax Years (Tax Years Beginning Before January 1, 2026): Completing Section G on Form 6765 is optional for all filers for the 2024 and 2025 tax years (Instructions for Form 6765, "What's New"; JLK Rosenberger; Leyton). However, taxpayers claiming or amending 2024 R&D credits must still report aggregate QREs in Section F and maintain underlying component-level books and records under IRC § 6001 to substantiate the Four-Part Test upon examination.

2026 Tax Year and Beyond (Tax Years Beginning After December 31, 2025): Section G becomes mandatory for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, for all filers unless they qualify for one of two narrow exemptions (Instructions for Form 6765).

body.text: 6.2 Mechanics of the "80% / Top 50" Rule and Small-Filer Exemptions
When completing Section G, taxpayers must itemize their QREs by individual business component in descending order of total QRE cost, continuing until the listed business components represent either:

items: At least 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48, OR
A maximum cap of 50 business components, whichever occurs first ("80%/Top 50" rule, Instructions for Form 6765; RK Partners).

body.text: For each reported business component, the taxpayer must disclose the component name, component type (product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention), and QREs broken down into direct conduct wages, direct supervision wages, direct support wages, supplies, leased computer costs, and contract research (RK Partners).
Only two categories of taxpayers are exempt from mandatory Section G reporting starting in 2026 (Instructions for Form 6765; EisnerAmper):

items: Qualified Small Businesses (QSBs) Electing the Payroll Tax Credit: Taxpayers qualifying as a QSB under IRC § 41(h)(3) (less than $5 million in current-year gross receipts and no gross receipts prior to the 5-tax-year period ending with the current tax year) that check the box on Form 6765 to apply a portion of their research credit against payroll taxes.

Small Filers on Original Returns: Taxpayers with total QREs (determined at the controlled-group level) of $1.5 million or less AND average annual gross receipts (for the prior three tax years under IRC § 448(c)(3), determined at the controlled-group level) of $50 million or less, provided the research credit is claimed on an original return (meaning amended returns do not qualify for this small-filer exemption).

body.text: 7. Comparative Evaluation of Market Compliance Methodologies for R&D Credit Calculation and Substantiation

The accuracy and audit survival of a 2024–2026 R&D tax credit calculation depend heavily on the compliance methodology used to link financial QRE allocations to technical Four-Part Test evidence. The compliance market divides into three primary operational models:
7.1 Big 4 Accounting Firms and Generalist CPA Practices

As documented in industry comparisons (including Boast.ai's market comparison and GrantOps' fee benchmark analysis), Big 4 and generalist CPA firms present structural trade-offs when preparing R&D credit calculations:

items: Fee Structure and Staffing: Big 4 engagements are oriented toward Fortune 500 and large enterprise clients and frequently carry high fixed or contingency fees (typically $30,000 to $40,000+ on a $200,000 claim, or $300 to $500+ per hour, per published industry benchmarks) while often delegating project interviews on mid-market engagements to generalist accounting staff rather than degreed engineers or scientists.

Reliance on Retrospective Estimates: Generalist practices frequently allocate wage QREs using post-year-end, retrospective percentage estimates rather than contemporaneous project tracking—an approach rejected by the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113.
Uninsured Hourly Audit Defense: Audit defense is typically billed separately on an open-ended hourly basis if the IRS examines the return.

body.text: 7.2 Self-Service Automated Software (SaaS) Platforms
Automated R&D software platforms integrate with payroll and accounting APIs to extract W-2 wage and general ledger figures rapidly at low subscription or percentage fees. However:

items: Qualitative Substantiation Gap: Pulling payroll registers by job title (e.g., "Software Engineer") calculates a financial number but does not establish technical uncertainty, a systematic process of experimentation, or subcomponent shrink-back boundaries under IRC § 41(d).

Shifted Engineering Burden: Purely self-service tools shift the burden of writing legally compliant Four-Part Test narratives back onto internal engineering teams, leaving claims vulnerable during IRS audits.

cells: High fixed/hourly fees; separate hourly audit billing
Hourly or contingent fees; separate hourly audit billing
Low subscription/percentage fee; limited live representation
